Plain-English Guide (2026)", "metaDescription": "Vibe coding means describing what you want in plain English and letting AI write the code. See where the term came from and how it applies to websites.", "targetKeyword": "what is vibe coding", "category": "Glossary", "bodyHtml": "

Short definition

Vibe coding is a way of building software where you describe what you want in plain, everyday language and an AI writes and iterates the actual code for you. Instead of typing out functions and markup line by line, you stay in a conversation: you say what you want to see or happen, the AI produces working code, you look at the result, and you ask for changes until it matches what's in your head. The "coding" still happens — it's just that the AI is the one typing.

Where the term comes from

"Vibe coding" was popularized in early 2025 by AI researcher Andrej Karpathy, who used it to describe a loose, conversational style of building with AI coding assistants: you describe the vibe of what you want, let the model generate the implementation, and steer by reacting to what comes back rather than reading every line. The phrase caught on fast because it named something a lot of people were already doing — using chat-based AI tools to build real software without treating every keystroke as sacred. By 2026 it's become the common shorthand for natural-language, AI-driven development in general, including tools built specifically for websites and apps.

A plain-language analogy

Think about the difference between building furniture by hand and describing what you want to a skilled carpenter. Traditional coding is like being the carpenter yourself: you cut every board, measure every joint, and if something's off, you go back and re-cut it. Vibe coding is more like telling that carpenter, "I want a bookshelf, about this wide, with a closed cabinet at the bottom, in a warm wood tone" — then looking at what they build, and saying "make the shelves a bit deeper" or "add a door there instead." You're not doing the joinery. You're directing the outcome, in your own words, and reacting to what shows up.

Why it matters

Vibe coding matters because it moves the bottleneck of building software from knowing how to write code to knowing what you want. That opens the door to a much wider set of people:

  • Non-developers — small business owners, marketers, designers, students — can produce real, working software without first learning a programming language.
  • Developers can move faster on the parts of a project that are more about assembly than deep engineering, freeing up time for the harder problems that still need hands-on code.
  • Ideas get tested sooner. A concept that used to take days to prototype can go from description to a working, clickable version in minutes, which changes how many ideas actually get tried.

It's not that code stops mattering — real code is still being written and run. What changes is who can direct that code getting written, and how quickly.

A real example

Say someone wants a landing page for a new pottery studio. In a vibe coding workflow, they don't open a code editor or pick a template. They type something like: "Build me a one-page site for a pottery studio called Clayworks — hero section with a class-signup button, a section showing our three class types, and a contact section with our studio address." The AI generates the actual page: real components, real layout, real styling. The person looks at it rendered live, then says "make the hero darker and move the class types above the fold" — and the AI updates the real code behind the page to match. No line of code was hand-typed by the person, but a working, structured site came out the other end.

How Kodely applies vibe coding to websites

Kodely is a vibe coding tool built specifically for websites. The workflow follows the pattern above directly:

  • You describe the site you want in a chat interface, in plain English.
  • Kodely generates a real Vite + React + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS application — actual component files, not a static template being filled in.
  • A live preview shows the actual compiled app as it's being built, so you're always looking at the real thing, not a mockup.
  • To make a change, you describe it in chat, the same way you'd redirect the carpenter in the analogy above, and Kodely edits the real components behind the scenes.
  • If a change doesn't work out, checkpoints let you roll back to a prior version for free, so experimenting has no downside.
  • If you want to see what the AI actually wrote, the code view shows the real generated source in-app.
  • When you're happy with it, one-click Publish puts the site live on a real public URL at <yourname>.kodely.site, included at no extra cost.

Today, Kodely focuses on the frontend — the part of vibe coding most people mean when they talk about building a site by describing it. You can start building for free: new accounts get 750 credits with no card required, and a build that fails to compile is never charged.

Related terms

  • What is an AI website builder? — the category of tool that vibe coding for websites usually runs on.
  • Prompt-to-app — a related term for going from a written description straight to a working application.
  • Natural-language programming — the broader idea of directing software behavior with everyday language instead of code syntax.

Try it yourself

The easiest way to understand vibe coding is to do it once. Sign up for Kodely and describe a site in plain English — you'll have a real, working page in front of you in a couple of minutes. If you want to see plans and credit pricing first, check out Kodely pricing, or browse more explainers like this one on the Kodely blog.
